newsitem.title: USA: Clinton decides to toughen U.S. air standards.
newsitem.headline: Clinton decides to toughen U.S. air standards.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton has decided to support controversial strict new air pollution standards proposed by the Environmental Protection Agency, a official of the Sierra Club pressure group said on Wednesday.

Kathryn Hohmann said she and other environmental advocates had been informed of the decision by the Clinton administration. "This is a clear victory that will clear the air," she told Reuters of the decision, which Clinton was expected to announce later on Wednesday.

Hohmann said that Clinton had endorsed the EPA's proposal to lower the 0.12 parts-per-million standard for smog-forming ozone to 0.08 parts-per-million. But the White House slightly eased, compared with what the EPA had proposed, the number of violations that would be allowed before an area was considered to be out of compliance with the standard.
The administration wholly backed EPA's proposed new standards for fine particles, she said.
"Bill Clinton and (Vice President) Al Gore have obviously made the decision to protect the 5 million American children who suffer from asthma from pollution in our air," she said.

EPA's proposal last November sparked a major controversy, with U.S. industry groups and some cities and states saying that controls needed to meet the new standards would be far too costly, and environmental and health advocates saying existing standards were too weak to protect children from lung diseases.
